prime.problem: Pair and window questions look like n² work: every pair, every window. On sorted data most of those candidates can be ruled out by a single comparison, but only if you move your indices in a way that never needs to go back.
prime.fits: Opens the Searching part because the next card's predicate uses its same-direction count. It builds on sorting (the whole technique needs order) and comes back in greedy wildcard matching and the source's skyline sweep.
prime.goal: Pick the right pointer shape for a problem, state the invariant that makes each move safe, and sweep intervals correctly at ties.

attend: In two-sum on sorted input, why may you drop a[hi] for good when a[lo] + a[hi] is too big?
In the pair-count scan, why does j never have to move back when i advances?
Why does merging intervals need them sorted by start, and what goes wrong without the sort?
At time 10 one meeting ends and another starts. Which event must sort first, and what count do you get otherwise?
Which condition must a window satisfy for the same-direction technique to be valid, and why do negative values break it?

must: Sorted input → if a[lo] + a[hi] > target, a[hi] is too big even with the smallest live partner → drop it; symmetric for too small → each step discards one candidate forever → ≤ n − 1 steps instead of n(n − 1)/2 pairs (5 vs 21 on a)
Same-direction scan: as a[i] grows, the first a[j] > a[i] + d can only move right → j never restarts → both pointers cross the array once → O(n) total moves (14, not 49, on a)

Sort intervals by start → any interval that overlaps the current block must start before its end → one sweep with a running end merges them; +1/−1 events with ends before starts at ties give the peak room count
elevated: Window validity must be monotone (shrinking a valid window keeps it valid) → true for non-negative values → with negatives, growing can lower the sum → use prefix sums with a monotonic deque or an ordered set instead
reference: the source's −n + Σ(j − i) counting form

compress.prompt: From memory, sketch the three shapes (opposite ends, same direction, interval sweep) as three tiny diagrams, and under each write the invariant that makes a move safe and why the total is O(n) after sorting.
checklist: opposite ends: the answer pair, if any, stays inside [lo, hi]
same direction: the stopping point of j is monotone in i
each pointer moves one way, so ≤ 2n moves
intervals: sort by start, keep a running end or a running count
ties: ends before starts when an end frees the room
needs sorted data or a monotone window condition

retrieve.q: Explain why two pointers find a sorted two-sum in O(n) without ever missing the answer.
answer: invariant: if a valid pair exists, both indices are in [lo, hi]
a sum too big means a[hi] can't pair with anything ≥ a[lo], so dropping it is safe (and symmetric for too small)
each step shrinks the range by one, so at most n − 1 steps

retrieve.q: Walk through counting pairs with a[j] − a[i] ≤ 10 in a = [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82] at i = 3 and i = 4: where does j stop, and what is added?
answer: i = 3 (27): j stops at 4 because 38 > 37; partners j − i − 1 = 0
i = 4 (38): j moves to 6 because 82 > 48; partner 43 → +1

retrieve.q: Classic two-sum: unsorted input, and you must return the original indices. Two pointers or a hash map? Cost of each, and what would flip your choice?
answer: two pointers need a sort: O(n log n) and you lose the original indices unless you carry them
hash map: one pass, O(n) time, O(n) memory
flip to two pointers when the data is already sorted, memory is tight, or the question is a range (pairs within d), which a hash map can't answer

compare.q: cs-1's sliding window and this card's same-direction scan both move two indices forward. What property of the window lets each index move only forward, and which problem shape breaks both?
answer: validity must be monotone: shrinking a valid window keeps it valid (or growing an invalid one keeps it invalid)
then the left edge's best position only moves right as the right edge grows
negative values break it for sums: growing the window can lower the sum, so a smaller left index can become valid again

compare.q: The merge step and the opposite-ends scan both walk two indices over sorted data. What is each deciding at every step, and why are both linear?
answer: merge: which front item is smaller, to output it
two-sum: which end can be ruled out, to discard it
in both, each step advances one pointer and no pointer goes back, so steps ≤ total length

predict.q: Meetings [1, 5], [2, 6], [5, 8], [6, 9]. Predict the number of rooms with ends sorted before starts at ties, and with starts before ends.
predict.answer: Ends first: 2 rooms (the meeting ending at 5 frees a room for the one starting at 5, and the same at 6). Starts first: the counts at times 5 and 6 briefly add the new meeting before removing the old one, so the peak wrongly reaches 3.

apply.task: On a = [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82], run opposite-end two-sum for target 37 and for target 100, writing each (lo, hi, sum, move). Then merge [[6, 8], [1, 9], [2, 4], [4, 7]] by the sort-then-sweep rule.
apply.done: Target 37 is found at indices (2, 3), 10 + 27, after 6 sums; target 100 has no pair and the scan stops after 6 sums with lo = hi. The intervals merge to [[1, 9]].
apply.hint: For 100: the first three sums (85, 91, 92) are too small, so lo moves three times before 27 + 82 = 109 finally moves hi.
